enrichment.short_title: Bankruptcy annulment refused where debtor could not pay creditors
key_facts: Mr Owo-Sampson was made bankrupt in June 1998 on a petition by Barclays Bank for unpaid taxed costs from earlier litigation.

The Court of Appeal held the bankruptcy order ought not to have been made because Barclays was fully secured on the debtor's property, but remitted the section 282 annulment discretion to the registrar.

The registrar refused annulment because proposed remortgage funds of about £325,000 would not cover the Bank of Scotland shared-appreciation mortgage (about £300,000), Barclays' debt, trustee expenses and other liabilities.
The debtor appealed the registrar's refusal; trustee-in-bankruptcy costs exceeded £77,000 plus DTI fees.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to a High Court judge from a bankruptcy registrar's refusal to annul a bankruptcy order under section 282(1)(a) Insolvency Act 1986, following Court of Appeal remittal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; registrar's exercise of discretion under section 282 upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a bankruptcy order ought not to have been made on the facts at the time, annulment under section 282 is discretionary; on appeal the court will not interfere unless the registrar took account of irrelevant material, ignored relevant material, or exercised discretion unreasonably. The court must be satisfied that annulment would not prejudice creditors and that the debtor can satisfy the petitioning creditor and meet other liabilities.
legal_issues: Whether the registrar erred in exercising discretion under section 282(1)(a)
Whether the debtor demonstrated ability to remortgage and pay secured and unsecured creditors if annulled
Whether Barclays should bear trustee-in-bankruptcy costs arising from reliance on obsolete Re Button authorities
Standard of review on insolvency appeals from registrars

enrichment.short_title: Crown Court wrongly refused adjournment when prosecution witnesses absent
key_facts: Simon Woodland appealed to Winchester Crown Court against a Basingstoke magistrates' conviction for obstructing a police constable.
The appeal was brought forward from 21 to 20 March 2003 without CPS knowledge; prosecution witnesses Emmerson, Hunt and Budgen could not attend at short notice.
Prosecuting counsel sought an adjournment but the Crown Court refused; the prosecution offered no evidence and the appeal was allowed.
Mrs Budgen had confirmed willingness to attend on the original Friday date but cited childcare difficulties for the brought-forward Thursday hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review by the Crown Prosecution Service of Winchester Crown Court's refusal to grant an adjournment on 20 March 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; Crown Court decision quashed; matter remitted for early relisting.
enrichment.ratio: Refusal of an adjournment where prosecution witnesses are absent is a case-management discretion reviewable only on Wednesbury grounds. Where the appellant had already been convicted on those witnesses' evidence, witnesses had confirmed attendance on the original date, and absence was not their fault, refusing adjournment to avoid delay was unreasonable; the court must balance interests of accused, victim and public.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of adjournment for absent prosecution witnesses was Wednesbury unreasonable
Application of triangulation of interests in criminal appeals
Weight to be given to delay where appeal had not previously been adjourned

enrichment.short_title: Village green registration quashed for user, locality and fairness flaws

statutes_considered.name: Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000

key_facts: Cheltenham Builders acquired land at Magpie Bottom, Hanham and sought planning permission for housing; local residents applied to register the land as a class (c) village green.

South Gloucestershire Council's committee accepted officer advice and registered the site in September 2002 despite objections that the land was overgrown, user was not as of right, and the delineated 'locality' was arbitrary.
The claimant challenged by judicial review and parallel section 14 Commons Registration Act proceedings.
The council had not held an oral hearing or non-statutory inquiry despite significant factual disputes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined judicial review and section 14 Commons Registration Act 1965 claim, tried as preliminary issues before Sullivan J.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded; registration decision held unlawful on grounds of user, locality, fairness and as-of-right user; relief reserved.
enrichment.ratio: Registration of a class (c) green requires proof on the balance of probabilities that the whole site was used for lawful sports and pastimes as of right for 20 years by a significant number of inhabitants of a genuine locality or neighbourhood. A locality is not any area drawn on a plan; where written evidence leaves extent and nature of user unresolved, acceptance without oral hearing is procedurally unfair; landowner objections ending in withdrawal of an earlier application can break 'as of right' user.
legal_issues: Whether the committee could reasonably find 20-year user of the whole overgrown site
Meaning of 'locality' and 'neighbourhood' under section 22(1A)
Whether registration could proceed without oral hearing where facts were disputed
Whether user continued as of right after landowner's objections to first application
Appropriate remedy: judicial review versus section 14

enrichment.short_title: Costs postponed under regulation 127 on agreed judicial review order
key_facts: Hertsmere Borough Council brought judicial review proceedings against the First Secretary of State and a second defendant.
The parties agreed consent order terms, amending paragraph 3 of the schedule by deleting words after a full stop following 'Luton'.
Costs remained in dispute; the second defendant (legally aided) was ordered to pay the claimant's costs incurred after 30 October 2003.
Determination of the amount of the second defendant's liability for costs was postponed for three years under regulation 127.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court hearing to approve agreed consent order and determine costs in judicial review proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Consent order approved as amended; second defendant ordered to pay claimant's post-30 October 2003 costs with three-year postponement of costs assessment under regulation 127.
enrichment.ratio: Where a publicly funded second defendant is ordered to pay a successful public authority claimant's costs, regulation 127 may be used instead of the 'normal order' limiting recovery to six years, to preserve the authority's ability to recover costs over a longer period; the court may limit costs to those incurred after a specified date where earlier costs are covered by the Treasury.
legal_issues: Appropriate costs order against legally assisted defendant in judicial review
Use of regulation 127 postponement versus normal six-year limitation
Limitation of costs to those incurred after 30 October 2003

enrichment.short_title: Prison Service adequately consulted on abolition of mandatory training
key_facts: Prison Service Instruction 09-2003 abolished central prescription of mandatory prison staff training and devolved decisions to local governors.
The Prison Officers' Association claimed breach of the legally binding Voluntary Agreement with the Prison Service for failure to consult adequately.
A 17 October 2002 letter enclosed a draft PSI and invited comments by 15 November; the POA attended a Training Forum on 6 November but made only brief objections.
The POA did not request more time or submit detailed representations before the PSI was issued on 4 February 2003; it later sought suspension and brought judicial review instead of arbitration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim by the Prison Officers' Association against the Secretary of State for the Home Department.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; consultation within the meaning of the Voluntary Agreement held to have been offered.
enrichment.ratio: Consultation under the Voluntary Agreement requires the Prison Service to initiate discussions and invite views on significant policy changes; it need not follow a prescribed forum. Where unions are invited to comment on a draft instruction, may attend a forum, and fail to make reasoned representations or seek extensions before implementation, adequate consultation has been offered even if the Service initially considered the matter outside the agreement.
legal_issues: Whether PSI 09-2003 fell within scope of the Voluntary Agreement
Whether consultation offered by letter and Training Forum satisfied the agreement
Whether status quo required suspension of the PSI after issue
Appropriateness of judicial review where arbitration clause existed

enrichment.short_title: Section 91(14) residence restriction set aside for lack of findings
key_facts: Dr P appealed paragraph 7 of Bennett J's order prohibiting further residence applications without leave under section 91(14).
The mother sought the order citing litigation stress and financial burden; only two rounds of residence litigation concerning child A were recorded.
Dr P gave evidence that a section 91(14) order was inappropriate and undertook not to make further applications if satisfied with the outcome.
Bennett J made the order limited to residence but not contact, without specific findings of serious risk of unacceptable strain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against one paragraph of a residence/contact order made at first instance in private law Children Act proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 91(14) order set aside; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where there is no history of repeated unreasonable applications, a section 91(14) order may still be made under Re P guidance only if the court finds the facts go beyond common post-order adjustment difficulties and that, absent the restriction, the child or primary carer faces a serious risk of unacceptable strain. Procedural objections based on absence of Form C2 fail where notice was clearly given; lack of specific findings on risk is fatal.
legal_issues: Procedural requirements for making a section 91(14) order
Application of Re P paragraphs 6 and 7 where no history of vexatious applications
Whether judge was obliged to reopen after draft judgment
Need for findings of serious risk of unacceptable strain

enrichment.short_title: Brussels II ousts European Convention enforcement of Paris contact order
key_facts: Italian parents divorced in Paris; the mother was permitted to relocate with the children to London in December 2002 with defined contact to the father.
Christmas and Easter contact failed; children refused to go with the father and displayed hostility.
The father sought enforcement in England under the 1980 European Convention on Recognition and Enforcement of Custody Decisions via the Central Authority.

Wall J registered and enforced the French order subject to phased London contact; the Court of Appeal held Brussels II Article 37 gave Brussels II precedence, rendering the section 16 summons a nullity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal against Wall J's registration and phased enforcement of a French contact order under the Child Abduction and Custody Act 1985; further argument on Brussels II Article 37.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal and cross-appeal disposed of by finding originating summons was a nullity; father must enforce under Brussels II or bring fresh Children Act proceedings.
enrichment.ratio: Contact orders made in matrimonial proceedings while the court retains parental-responsibility jurisdiction fall within Brussels II and must be enforced under that Regulation, not the 1980 European Convention, by virtue of Article 37 precedence. Article 11(2) permits phased implementation without reviewing the substance of the foreign order where Article 10 defences fail. Article 10(1)(a) and (b) grounds must be applied stringently.
legal_issues: Whether Article 10(1)(a) or (b) permitted refusal of enforcement
Whether Wall J's phased contact programme was implementation under Article 11(2) or impermissible review under Article 9(3)
Whether Brussels II Article 37 rendered European Convention enforcement proceedings a nullity
Whether the 11 December 2002 Paris order was 'given on the occasion of matrimonial proceedings'

enrichment.short_title: Fugitive libel claimant denied video-link evidence order
key_facts: Roman Polanski sued Conde Nast over a Vanity Fair article alleging callous conduct after Sharon Tate's murder.
He pleaded guilty in California in 1977 to unlawful sexual intercourse with a 13-year-old and fled before sentencing; he lives in France and will not enter the UK.
Eady J ordered he could give evidence by video link from Paris under CPR 32.3; the defendants appealed.
The Court held refusal of VCF would not permit hearsay statements where the claimant refused to attend for cross-examination.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against Eady J's interlocutory direction permitting claimant to give trial evidence by video conference link from Paris.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; VCF direction set aside; court indicated statements would be excluded if claimant refused to attend for cross-examination.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 32.3 VCF is an indulgence, not the norm. Where a claimant voluntarily brings libel proceedings in England, has pleaded guilty to a serious offence abroad and fled to avoid sentence, and seeks VCF solely to avoid arrest, the court should refuse VCF after weighing offence, link between claim and offence, party status, alternative forums and trial fairness. Article 6 is not infringed where access is conditional on attending to give live evidence.
legal_issues: Discretion to order evidence by video link under CPR 32.3
Whether fugitive status and extradition risk justify VCF
Exclusion of hearsay under CPR 32.1 and 33.4 if witness refuses cross-examination
Article 6 right of access and proportionality
Distinction from Rowland v Bock

enrichment.short_title: Asylum certification upheld; state protection threshold aligned with Article 3

statutes_considered.name: Geneva Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Lithuanian Roma claimant Mr Bagdanavicius and his wife claimed asylum and Article 3/8 protection, alleging harassment and violence from the wife's brother and associates.
The Secretary of State certified the claims as clearly unfounded under section 115(2002 Act), denying in-country appeal rights.
Maurice Kay J dismissed judicial review; the Court of Appeal considered relationship between Refugee Convention 'well-founded fear' and Article 3 'real risk', and sufficiency of state protection.
Post-decision and fresh evidence did not show an arguable case that an adjudicator would allow the claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from dismissal of judicial review of section 115 certification of asylum and ECHR claims as clearly unfounded.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; certification upheld; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: There is broad symmetry between the asylum test of well-founded fear of persecution and the Article 3 test of real risk of ill-treatment; sufficiency of state protection is systemic willingness and ability to provide reasonable protection, not a guarantee of safety. Section 115 certification requires that the claim could not on any legitimate view succeed; detailed substantive refusal reasons may suffice without separate certification reasoning. Section 65(1999 Act) did not create a lower human-rights risk threshold.
legal_issues: Relationship between well-founded fear and Article 3 real risk
Meaning and application of sufficiency of state protection
Effect of Soering on non-state actor cases
Lawfulness of section 115 clearly unfounded certification
Admissibility of post-decision and fresh evidence on appeal

enrichment.short_title: Planning appeal challenge dismissed as merits rerun on flat 7 retention
key_facts: Foley Court, Finchley comprised a three-storey block of six flats plus an unlawfully erected fourth-floor flat 7, subject to a long enforcement history from 1989.
Meritgold sought planning permission to retain flat 7 with alterations including height reduction, mansard-style cladding and revised fenestration.
An inspector dismissed the appeal in May 2002, finding flat 7 remained visually obtrusive and out of scale despite cosmetic improvements.
The claimant sought section 288 quashing on multiple grounds alleging the inspector failed to consider evidence and placed wrong weight on factors.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 application to quash inspector's dismissal of planning appeal; adjournment refused.
enrichment.outcome: Adjournment refused; section 288 application dismissed; claimant ordered to pay Secretary of State's costs (summarily assessed at about £4,000).
enrichment.ratio: Section 288 is not a merits rehearing. Allegations that an inspector gave insufficient weight to material considerations or disagreed with the applicant's planning view raise no error of law where the inspector addressed the factors and exercised planning judgment after site inspection. Weight is for the inspector, not the court.

Whether describing alterations as 'cosmetic' was legally flawed
Whether section 288 permits challenge to planning merits
